This page is for contributors to `scgsim.palace` run preparation and result
reading, and to the AEDT result views. It records which files a Palace run
writes and reads back, how result reading decides which folder holds which
pass, which records carry the margin rows, and what the views check before
they show a number. What each view shows a user is on
[Reading a run: the three views](../../reference/specs/report-model.qmd); the
Palace setup a user makes is on [Palace Electrostatic](../../reference/specs/palace-electrostatic-sgb.qmd)
and [Palace Eigenmode](../../reference/specs/palace-eigenmode.qmd).

## Which folder holds which pass {#pass-folders}

An AMR pass is one Palace solve, counted from 1: pass 1 solves the input mesh.
Which folder of `results/palace` holds which pass is decided by what its files
are, once, for the trust report and the convergence check alike:

- `iteration<k>/` is pass $k$ when its own `palace.json` records
  `Problem.Iteration` $k$ and its tables are regular files. Palace 0.18.1 moves
  the tables of solve $k$ there before it refines again.
- The top level is a pass of its own only when its `palace.json` and every table
  are regular files with data rows; its number is the iteration it records. This
  is the last solve of a run that ended by itself.
- A top level whose tables are links into `iteration<k>/` holds pass $k$'s
  files, not a solve of its own: a run stopped right after pass $k$. One that
  mixes links with new files, or holds a table with its header only, is a
  solve under way and is no pass.
- Two folders that record the same pass are one pass when they hold the same
  tables, byte for byte (a stopped run copied by a tool that follows links).
  Otherwise their readings conflict and that pass is not read.
- A folder whose own record is missing, unreadable or names another pass is no
  pass. No number is ever taken from a folder's place in the listing.
- A table that cannot be read (no permission, or bytes that are not text) does
  not stop the listing. A top level that holds one is set aside with the reason;
  two folders of one pass that cannot be compared for it leave that pass unread;
  a declared number in such a table is unavailable at that pass. The other
  folders are read all the same.

Every AMR pass axis of the trust report counts this way. A change is measured
only between two readable passes whose numbers are consecutive. The verdict
names the passes read, the passes before it that were not read, and every
folder set aside or pass not read, with why.

## Partly returned runs {#partly-returned-runs}

`inspect_run_trustworthiness()` supports completed, failed, and partly returned
run folders. It preserves the recorded receipt status and may expose the latest
readable evidence without promoting an incomplete run. The strict
`resolve_palace_result(..., expected_handoff_id=...)` path accepts only a
completed run folder whose handoff, receipt, solver, and artifact hashes validate.

A number that cannot be read without ambiguity (a table that repeats a column,
or two rows with the same index) is unavailable, with the reason, and never
holds. A plan that is present but was not sealed by the handoff, or that
changed after it, is refused by both readers.

## Margin rows of Palace Surface EPR {#palace-margin-rows}

The existing inspection and strict-resolution split also governs Palace margin
rows. A margin row is a `Dielectric` row over the bands SGB cut at and beyond
that margin, so it sits in the same `surface-Q.csv` table as the baseline rows.
`inspect_run_trustworthiness()` may inspect a completed, failed, or partly
returned run folder and marks unavailable margin data as unavailable without changing the
receipt state. Each source reads its margin rows as one all-or-nothing snapshot:
if its table cannot be read or does not match the index map, that source has no
margin snapshot. A strict completed resolution of a run that requested surface
rows requires the sealed `surface-Q.csv` from the same required result source;
a missing file prevents strict resolution, and an existing receipt or artifact
SHA-256 mismatch remains fatal.

`PhysicsQuantitiesReport.snapshots` remains the baseline-only surface. The typed
`PhysicsQuantitiesReport.margin_snapshots` surface exposes
`SurfaceMarginEprSeriesSnapshot` values, each holding
`SurfaceMarginEprRecord` rows with the interface, margin value (`margin_um`) and
ordinal (`margin_index`), the baseline row it belongs to (`baseline_index`), the
bands it covers, its entities and Nets, the mode or excitation, the refinement
pass, the native index and the source identity. Each margin row is one of several
alternatives to its baseline row; duplicate requested margins stay separately
traceable and are never duplicate contributions to a loss total.

## What the EPR views check {#epr-view-checks}

Scientific keys, not display labels, identify plotted data. Shared readable
labels appear across figures; hover data and metadata retain full group,
members, side, and source identity.

An AEDT `ResolvedRun` provides `epr_result()` for its bound EPR record and
`show_all_results(show_details=False)` for the integrated run view; the latter
returns `None`. The view uses all requested modes at the actual last completed
pass and includes the adaptive history. Missing or partial values remain
unavailable; presentation does not fall back to an earlier complete pass. It
checks consumed result CSVs and benchmark data against hashes captured during
resolution, without consulting a live simulation object or rereading native
AEDT state. See the
[AEDT runtime reference](aedt-runtime.qmd) for strict resolution and
missing-artifact behavior.

Adaptive frequency has its own availability rule: a finite, positive numeric
value that is not a boolean is plotted even when that mode's EPR row is partial.
Participation and energy still require a complete row; row status, integrity
checks, pass selection, and gaps in the plotted history remain unchanged.

Palace and AEDT quantities resolved from original run folders remain bound to
their applicable receipt, artifact-hash, handoff, and solver identities. A
detached Palace EPR result retains original artifact identity and hash
references, but those references do not authenticate the detached JSON itself.
Presentation does not weaken source bindings and makes no
numerical-convergence or cross-solver-agreement claim.

## Mesh context of a Palace report {#palace-mesh-context}

The Palace report reads the same detached `mesh_summary()` authority exposed by
the facade and resolved run. It binds the recorded sizing recipe, repair policy,
mesher options, quality threshold and the minSICN measured on the linear mesh
(before any elevation), together with the Gmsh version, native node/element/region
counts, the order of the delivered mesh, high-order optimization outcome and edge
length statistics, to the mesh and manifest identities. For elevated geometric
order, reported edge lengths are primary-corner chords rather than curved-edge
lengths. The Eigenmode degree-of-freedom value is a topological estimate, not a
solver-reported count.

## Palace run records {#palace-run-records}

### The dry-run preflight {#palace-preflight}

Before a generated script starts the solve, the exact copied `config.json` is
passed to the selected Palace executable with its native `--dry-run` option.
Only a successful dry-run of those exact bytes establishes config/runtime
compatibility. The compatibility artifact and returned receipt preserve the
config hash and observed native GitTag. When the configured executable is
directly and truthfully resolvable as the Palace binary, its basename and
SHA-256 are also retained. SCGSim does not inspect behind a wrapper to discover
its hidden binary. GitTag, commit, and any available binary hash are provenance
for reproducibility and diagnosis; their presence or value is not a
runtime-eligibility Gate.

If this preflight fails, the returned receipt records
`execution_stage="config_compatibility"`, `solver_invoked=false`, its separate
preflight and pipeline exit codes, and `solver_exit_code=null`. Receipts use
`execution_stage="solver"` only after the solver command was actually invoked.

### Staged state of a simulation {#staged-state}

Configuration setters are atomic with respect to this staged state. Route,
mesh and Eigenmode controls validate every supplied value before changing any
field. A validation failure therefore preserves the prior
configuration together with cached mesh, resolved-port, config, and handoff
state. A successful change retains the existing mesh/config invalidation
boundary; this does not change operational failures inside `mesh()` or
`write_config()`.

Shared staged invalidation and per-file persistence are described under
[the architecture](../architecture.qmd#palace-preparation-lifecycle).
Invalidation is not a promise of whole-workflow atomic disk replacement.

### Attributes and the mesh manifest {#mesh-manifest}

The run folder holds the SGB model (`geometry/`, with the XAO and its sidecar),
the meshing report (`mesh/`, as JSON and text), `palace.msh` and the mesh
manifest (`metadata/`). `palace.msh` is a Gmsh MSH 2.2 ASCII file, the format
Palace reads. Palace lowers SGB's named groups to solver attributes from the
sidecar alone: it splits a surface group only where its faces are integrated by
different Surface-EPR rows or sides, so the attributes partition the faces and
nothing is counted twice. Electrical identity is the Net; the Terminal and
Ground bindings use the exact Net of the sidecar.

The mesh manifest (`schema_version` 2) records the route and its policy, the
sidecar schema and model identity digest, the Surface-EPR inset requests with
the band families they produced and the faces SGB skipped, the recipe (name,
version and parameters), repair policy, mesher options, budgets and threshold,
the path and SHA-256 of the quality report, and one entry per solver attribute
with the SGB group it came from. It also records the Gmsh version, node and
element types, physical-region element counts and edge-length statistics. Edge
lengths for high-order meshes are explicitly labeled as primary-corner chords
and reported in micrometres; they are not curved-edge arc lengths.

Both Palace facades and a resolved Palace run expose `mesh_summary()`. It returns
a detached value bound to the mesh and manifest identities. The Palace report
reads this same summary authority. Eigenmode includes an Nédélec topological
degree-of-freedom estimate based on primary-corner tetrahedron topology and the
configured FEM order. It is not an actual solver degree-of-freedom count;
changing FEM order updates the estimate without remeshing. Electrostatic's
H1 estimate is unavailable. No SCGSim record measures the quality of curved
high-order elements.

### Mesh version identities {#mesh-version-identities}

A recipe's version goes up only when the sizes it asks for change. `FeatureRecipe`
went from `features/1` to `features/2` when it began to size every Surface-EPR
band boundary curve, and to `features/3` when it began to size the outline of
every Route A conductor sheet. So two reports with the same recipe version and the same
parameters asked for the same initial sizes, even when they were made by
different package releases; a different recipe version means the meshes were
made by different sizing rules. The recipe version covers the initial sizes
only: the repair policy is recorded in each report, and the Gmsh version in the
mesh manifest.

The versions are separate because one version for the whole meshing module
would change whenever any recipe changed, and could not say which one did. A
run with `UniformBoundaryRecipe` keeps its version when `FeatureRecipe` changes,
so its reports stay comparable across that change.

For example, the same default `FeatureRecipe()` on a flip-chip qubit with bands
of 0.5 and 1 µm (the OrcaPen SC PDK `disk_flip_chip_qubit` under common ground
planes, Route B) gives two different meshes under the two versions:

::: {.askr-table-compact}
| | `scgsim.meshing.features/1` | `scgsim.meshing.features/2` |
|---|---|---|
| Sizes asked for | 1.30 µm on the 801 film-wall curves | 1.30 µm on 3,104 curves: the film walls and every band boundary curve |
| First mesh | 402,784 tetrahedra, 1 below the quality threshold | 569,325 tetrahedra, none below it |
| Result | clean after one repair round: 407,093 tetrahedra, 82.5 s | clean in the first mesh: 569,325 tetrahedra, 53.4 s |
:::

The two quality reports name different recipe versions, so the different mesh
comes from the sizing rules, not from anything else in the run.

### Index map rows, sides and cracked sheets {#index-map-rows}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Rows, sides and cracked sheets"}
The index map (schema v3) records, for each surface row, its `row` and `group`,
`interface_type`, `band`, `side`, `face_sides`, `entities`, `net` and
`attributes`, and the lineage membership as attribution only: lineage weights
nothing. A one-sided row maps `above` or `below` to Palace's postprocessing side.
A Route A sheet with vacuum on both sides is one face integrated from both sides,
which needs Palace's internal-boundary cracking; SCGSim writes
`Model.CrackInternalBoundaryElements` exactly when a configured row has a
`shared_face_group`, so a run that configures no `MA` or `MS` film on a sheet
keeps Palace's default. A sheet over vacuum and dielectric in different places gives
separate `MA` and `MS` rows on different attributes.
:::

### Surface-film producer {#surface-film-producer}

Surface-film inputs bind exact source surfaces and physical attributes to the
Palace `MA`, `MS`, or `SA` type and its film assumptions. Provide exactly one
of `thickness` (native model units) or `film_thickness_m` (converted using
`Model.L0`), and exactly one of numeric `permittivity` or `material_id` that
resolves to an explicit dielectric. `loss_tangent` may be supplied directly or
read from that material; an unknown value remains distinguishable in SCGSim's
index. The current `surface-film.v2` producer rejects missing or duplicated
surface and physical-attribute identities rather than dropping or deduplicating
them. Film thickness sets the surface model, and
[inset margins](../../reference/specs/palace-eigenmode.qmd#surface-epr-margins) set any requested exclusion near the gaps.

Palace 0.18.1 forms native surface integrands from the configured type and the
neighboring solution elements: `MA` and `SA` use the vacuum-side trace, while
`MS` uses the substrate-side trace. `MA` uses normal electric field, `MS` uses
the substrate-permittivity-weighted normal field, and `SA` combines tangential
and normal terms with the film permittivity. See Palace 0.18.1's
[configuration](https://github.com/awslabs/palace/blob/0dc74cdf8c36c58b69b21c4a06e816048ec0b83f/palace/utils/configfile.cpp#L624)
and [neighbor-material rules](https://github.com/awslabs/palace/blob/0dc74cdf8c36c58b69b21c4a06e816048ec0b83f/palace/fem/coefficient.hpp#L331)
for the native mapping. Choose `MA`, `MS`, or `SA` to match the
intended native interface model.

### The convergence plan {#convergence-plan-record}

With a declaration, the declared criteria take the place of Palace's own
tolerance. `write_config()` writes `Model.Refinement.Tol` as the smallest normal
double, so that only `amr_max_passes` ends the run, and
`SaveAdaptIterations: true`, so that Palace keeps every pass in
`results/palace/iteration<k>`. It writes the plan of the check to
`metadata/palace_convergence_plan.json`: for each criterion its label as the
report shows it, and for each number the result table, the row, the columns and
how they combine (a participation sums the columns of its rows), the test, the
threshold, and `minimum_converged_passes`. Which columns make up a quantity is
decided there once, from the index map entries the same config writes.
`prepare_handoff()` seals the plan with the other inputs, so a returned run with
a changed plan is refused. Without a declaration nothing of this is written and
the config is what the AMR controls alone give.

### The convergence runner {#convergence-runner}

The run script starts the solver command through the convergence runner,
`metadata/run_palace_until_converged.py`, which `prepare_handoff()` copies
into the run folder and which needs only Python's standard library. The
runner:

1. starts the solver command the script would have run, in a session of its
   own; Palace's output reaches the log as before;
2. looks at `results/palace` every second. A pass counts once its
   `iteration<k>/` folder is unchanged between two looks, and after each new pass
   the runner runs the same check that result reading runs;
3. when the verdict is converged, writes
   `metadata/palace_convergence_decision.json` first, then sends SIGTERM to the
   solver's session and waits until all of it has ended: the command, the
   launcher it started and the ranks the launcher ends. If any of it is still
   running 60 s later, it sends SIGKILL;
4. when the solver has ended, after the stop or by itself at `amr_max_passes`,
   writes the decision record again with the passes `results/palace` then holds
   and the solver's exit code.

The runner does not leave the solver running unwatched. Told to end (SIGTERM,
SIGINT or SIGHUP), it ends the solver first and records why. Ended without that
chance (SIGKILL, to the runner or to the script's whole process group), it
leaves the solver to its guard: a process the runner starts with the solver, in
a session of its own, which ends the solver's session in the same way once the
runner is gone.

Palace 0.18.1 completes pass $k$ in `iteration<k>/` before it refines the mesh
for pass $k+1$, so the stop comes during that refinement or at the start of the
next solve; no file of a completed pass changes. The stop is requested one to
two seconds after the folder appears (the runner looks every second and counts a
pass at its second look), and Palace has ended within about a second of the
request. The receipt is written only then, so no solver process writes a file
after it.

A pass that takes less than those one to two seconds still runs. The runner then
counts it with the pass before it: the verdict names the pass at which the run
converged and how many passes were read after it, Palace is stopped after the
last of them, and the result is that last pass. A run whose passes are all that
short has ended before the runner looked; it is complete as Palace ended it.
What the stop saves is every pass longer than that, which is where the time
goes: a pass has two to three times the elements of the one before.

The receipt states how the solver ended (`ending`) and keeps the solver's own
exit code:

| `ending` | When | Receipt |
|---|---|---|
| `solver_ended` | Palace ended without a stop from SCGSim | `completed` when every exit code is 0, `failed` otherwise |
| `stopped_at_convergence` | the runner stopped it after a pass at which the verdict is converged, and it ended within the wait | `completed`, with the exit code the stop gave: 143 for Palace's `palace` wrapper script, which the signal ends, 1 for `mpirun` started directly, and 137 for `srun`, which ends its step |
| `stop_escalated` | it did not end on SIGTERM and was killed | `failed` |
| `runner_terminated` | the runner itself was told to end and ended Palace for that reason. Told to end while Palace is already ending after the stop at convergence, the stop stands | `failed` |
| `not_recorded` | the runner left no complete decision record | `failed` |

The result of a run stopped at convergence is its last pass: result reading
takes the tables and the cost from `iteration<k>/`, since the top level holds
links into it or a solve under way. Palace can also complete its last solve in
the moment the runner decides. If it has ended by itself by then (exit code 0,
its last solve at the top level), nothing was stopped and the run is recorded
as ended by itself. If the stop still reaches it, the run was stopped and its
result is that last solve, at the top level.

Result reading computes the check again from the returned files and refuses
the run, naming what disagrees, when:

- the passes or the verdict differ from the decision record, or the record is
  not the one the receipt binds;
- the decision record and the receipt state different endings, or different
  exit codes of the solver;
- the top level holds links or a solve under way, and the receipt says Palace
  ended by itself;
- a decision record is present without a plan, or a plan has none;
- a table of the result, at the top level or in `iteration<k>/`, is not among
  the outputs the receipt records.

On Slurm the command after `--` is the `srun` line, and the scheduler writes
the log. The runner starts that command in a session of its own and stops it
with SIGTERM once the declared criteria have converged; `srun` answers by
ending its step, so the Palace tasks are killed and `srun` exits with 137. The
script then exits with the receipt's verdict (0 for a
completed run), because a solver stopped at convergence exits non-zero although the run completed. It
also removes an earlier `metadata/palace_convergence_decision.json` before the
solve. Without a declaration the script is unchanged: it starts the solver
command itself.
